titleStmt.title: Interview with Herbert Cohan, 11/10/2017
titleStmt.author: Dave Sullivan and Deborah A. Boreson [transcriber]

bibl.title: Interview with Herbert Cohan
bibl.author: Dave Sullivan and Deborah A. Boreson [transcriber]

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Herbert Cohan was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. Today is November 10th, 2017. We are in Waukegan, Illinois today at the courthouse, and we are in Courtroom 204. Weare interviewing today -- do you want to go by Herb or Herbert?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Herb is easy.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Herb is okay. Herbert Cohan.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Who was a Navy veteran and is going to give us a history today of all the things he has done which is a plethora of things that he has accomplished in his lifetime. We are very glad we are able to sit down and get all this information. You understand this will be sent -- the court reporter will give you a copy of this eventually. You will get a picture, and we are going to send all this to the archives in Washington. So there will be a permanent record down there of all the things you have done in your lifetime. Anytime anybody wants to look you up, they can. When were you born, Herb?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: December 3rd, 1926.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. And today with us is Herb, of course myself, I am Dave Sullivan, and the court reporter Debbie Boreson. Debbie, thank you. His son Brian is here with him too.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: He also has three other boys, Michael, Neal, and Paul who are in various parts of the country, but they are not here today. Now you are pretty much retired now, Herb?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I retired in 1986.I am sorry. Let me correct that.Iretired five and ahalf years ago. Just retired.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. So you have been working ever since, your whole lifetime just about, right?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Good. Now what branch of the service were you in?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: U.S. Navy.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: When were you in first? I think you were in a couple of times.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I was in World War II at the age of 17 with a parental signature. You needed to get a parental signature at that time.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Didn't you say you went to enlist, and they sent you home?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: They sent me home because I was too young.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Then what happened?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I went back with my mother's signature on there and joined the Navy and took my training up in Sampson Training Base in upper state New York near Canada. And then I went on to Schumaker, California for embarkation, and I was on board the Landing Ship Tank 119 for amphibious landing practice. It was on the beachheads, and I was on the Landing Ship Tank for a while when I got transferred to Whidbey Island, Washington off the coast for the purpose of going to the air station. And then we went on to Alaska, 200 miles from the Russian coast so we could scour it very well.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Nowyou just graduated high schoolwhenyou signed up?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I was 17. I got out of high school. I just got on the train, the street car actually in Boston.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: And then the elevator train went to the main post office to -- to the Naval Recruiting Center.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: So you are a fellow Bostonian then?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes, I was born and brought up in Boston.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: We park our car in Harbor Yard, don't we?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I can park the car in Harbor Yard.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: What rank were you, Herb?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Seaman.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Seaman. Okay. Where did you serve? You started out in New York in boot training, right?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Where did you go from there?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Schumaker, California. Okay. LST, Landing Ship Tank 119, and then to Whidbey Island.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. How long were you in the first time?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: From 1944 to 1946.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. Then in 1946, then what happened?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Then I came back to Boston. I went into the restaurant business. My dad was in the restaurant business in Boston.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: And in fact you are familiar with Boston. You knew it pretty well. Where the State House is, I had a coffee house behind the State House on George Street, and my dad and I had several restaurants. And they really didn't appeal to me so I asked him, talked to my dad, and even though that was not a desirable thing for him, I separated myself from the restaurant business, and took a politically appointed job for the City of Boston. And I worked there and found that not to be my career desires. I then entered the airline business with an airline called Capitol Airlines which is named after the Capitol of Washington, D.C. It originally came from Pennsylvania Central, and I worked for Capitol, and then I moved to Chicago. I moved to Chicago in 1951 at Midway Airport when Midway was the world's busiest airport at that time, and I worked at Midway during the entire time until it was ready to close when I moved to O'Hare.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: What did you do at Midway?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I did several things. I started out in customer service. I also worked -- had a crew that loaded the airplanes, and I learned the airline business from the ground up. I would like to go back a little bit.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: If you don't mind.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Please do.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: When I came out of the military in 1946, I knew a fellow who was closely associated with the hotel business near Fenway Park where the Red Sox played. A lot of people don't know this, the Atlanta Braves today were the Milwaukee Braves, they were the Boston Braves.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: And the Boston Bees.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: The Bees before the Boston Braves, and it didn't move to Milwaukee until years later when Lou Perini, the contractor, bought them and took them there.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: The three Little Steam Shovels.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Right. Now earlier before that in 1946 when I got discharged, thefellow Iknew in the hotel business came upto meandsays youdeserve to go to the World Series.Thatwasthe yearthe Braves won the National Leaguepennant.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes, and I went to watch Bob Feller from the Cleveland Indians pitch against Warren Spahn and two Hall of Fame pitchers, and I sat behind Bud Abbott and Lou Costello, the comedians, and had a great time. I don't know if I appreciated it as much as I would appreciate it today, but I had a great time. That was a present from him to me for coming home, and I did that.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: And the Braves lost the World Series to the Cleveland Indians.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: The Cleveland Indians.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: I still think Masi wasn't out. Anyway, okay. So now we are going to move you to --

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Then I went --

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: To O'Hare.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: O'Hare.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I went to O'Hare, but prior to coming to Chicago, I met my wife in Boston through somebody else that was working for the city, and we dated. Irene became an American Airlines stewardess, not a flight attendant. They called them stewardesses, and I began dating her again when she came to the school in Chicago at Midway. They had a training center, and we dated. And she moved to San Francisco for a while and then came back to Chicago. And we started dating again, and we got married at St. Rita's Church on the southwest side of Chicago at 63rd and Lawndale and Washtenaw. Father Luke Sweeney married us. We got secretly married in the court because there were rules and regulations that the first day of marriage, you lost your job. You weren't allowed to work anymore. They had to sign a contract. A lot of people don't know that. That was were the rules at that time.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: For the --

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: For a stewardess.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: For a stewardess.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: You had to leave your job. The only thing that made her leave her job eventually was pregnancy with my oldest son, but we did that. And then we did not move to where I am today in Arlington Heights until the closing of Midway Airport, and that's what brought me to live in Arlington Heights because I was driving a distance from the south side every day.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Was that in 1960?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: After Capitol Airlines moved into the merger with United Airlines, I became part of United Airlines. I worked in the airline business in many capacities, maintenance, and I was head of the Cargo Division at O'Hare when we had the old freighters.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I don't know if you know the airlines freight ships, and we had 28 freighters a night for O'Hare of DC-8s and quick change 727s. We took the seats out every night and moved cargo all night long, and then put the seats back in in the morning. It didn't work out too well because we were doing more damage to airplanes than we were making money, but I enjoyed the Cargo Division, and I spent the next -- just short of 36 years with United Airlines and retired. I took my early retirement because of a job offer for a Canadian company, Livingston International outside of Toronto, Etobicoke, and I covered the U.S.A. trying to build up their business.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Let's back up a little bit now. It is 1947. You are married, right?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Married.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: You are working at O'Hare?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: O'Hare, no.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: At Midway still?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I am still at Midway.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Then when did you go back in the service again?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I can't remember the exact date of entry, but I gave you the discharge for that.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: About 1946?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I got out in 19 -- let's see. I had eight years. I had eight years in there.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Eight years in there.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: You got out in 1946.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: The discharge shows it.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Then you went back?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I am going to say --

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Youwent back. Gotout in 1954,the second time,right?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I think that's what the date is.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: But when did you go back in? In other words, you got out in 1946, right?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: And I got married.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Had a family.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Then you went back in the service again, in the navy?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: The reserves.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: The reserves, right. You are in the reserves until 1954, right?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Where did you --

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Great Lakes.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Great Lakes. Okay. Which is right by Waukegan here. We are right close to that?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: In the reserves only.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Now what did that consist of, Herb? In other words, how much activity did you have?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Not a great deal except to give some people the experiences of your time to the younger folks coming in.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Now was that something you did like had to do two weeks in the summer? In the summer you had meetings every month or something like that?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yeah, it was very -- the only time it would be if there were a conflict and something happened, you signed up. You could be activated.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Right. You were never activated?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I wasn't activated.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: But you did serve all that time?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: All that time.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Until 1954 you were like on active duty two weeks in the summer time?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. And then you would have meetings like once a month?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yeah. Yes, sir. That's right.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: And you did it right here?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: It was a simple thing except for the thing it was -- the only danger behind that job was the fact that I had a family already and if I were activated.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yeah. Now did your family move up when you were here in north Chicago, did they come up? Did they leave or stay there?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: No, we stayed there.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: You stayed in Chicago?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. Now during the time that you were in the naval reserve, you were with Capital Airlines at the time?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: No, that was all United.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: That was United then?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: It was all merged already.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: So what did you do with United?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: United, I did several things. I was in their Maintenance Overhaul Division. I was in customer service. I was in ramp service, and I was in charge of all the cargo at O'Hare. Took 28 freighters a night, plus all the movement of all the cargoes. I had about -- at that time I had 430 people.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Wow, you were a busy guy.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: It was a busy Cargo Division.I seemed to havebeenenjoying logistics and cargo.For some reason,thatintrigued me the most. And when I retired, I did that for the purpose of staying in logistics with the Canadian company, but some of the promises I was made weren't fulfilled and without that, the phone rang one day and I joined two other fellows who had started a freight company that I knew ten years before, and they were a small company. We took that company from the time I joined them until the time I left from 1.2 million a year to 360 million.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Wow, pretty good.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Well, the company just sold and is still private. They are international. They had many stations, international. If you are enjoying something in life -- and I still do some mentoring of people. There are two people I am still mentoring. They are on the side, and it is a fulfillment you have inside you that you need to give some of that good information of how to -- without becoming overbearing with them. If they don't want some of the things, then that was just no cost. If you want to work with me, call me up on the phone and I will give you all the time I can. I am still doing two people right now.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Let me back up a minute now. The first time you went in the navy, 18 years old, 17 years old?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I was 17 years old.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Off to boot camp.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Then where did you go? How long were you there?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: In Sampson?

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Just through boot camp.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: They moved you right away.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Then where did you go?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Schumaker, California, embarkation point.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: What was your job there?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: In Schumaker?

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: You just did a multitude of things waiting for an assignment.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: It is an embarkation station, and if you are not familiar with that, you have to read the mustard board everyday. And if you see your name up there, it tells you where you are going.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Did you see your name one day?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes, and I did the wrong thing.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: There was a -- this is almost humorous. There was a sign up on the board saying Dive Bomber School. I said that would be a fascinating job. Dive bomber was a stick and a nail, and you pick up papers all day. I got my experience really quick. Don't volunteer for anything.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Did you get that job?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: How long did you do that?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Three days.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Then what came next?

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Landing Ship Tank, if you have ever seen a Landing Ship Tank, it is a very overcrowded, boarded ship, and the front comes down, and the tanks roll up for the beachhead. They were continually practicing beachhead landings with the dynamite crew, and I worked with the dynamite crew for a while.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Where was this, sir?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Off the coast of California.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: California?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Down by --

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: They don't tell you where you are. They just -- they just don't give you a point.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. Now what was your job on the -- was it the LST?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Carry dynamite.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Was it a LST?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: LST, L-S-T.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: What was your job?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Carrying the dynamite everyday, wiring it. They practiced beachhead landings.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: So you leave from there?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: From there.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: And where would you go?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: To Whidbey Island off the coast of Washington. I will tell you exactly where Whidbey Island is. Between Seattle and British Columbia, Vancouver. It is the halfway point. You go about 80 miles north of Seattle, and you go over Deception Pass of Oak Harbor. In Oak Harbor, it is full of naval patrolboats. Ofcourse, that was the PBYs,and PB4Y2s, andthey wouldshuffle crews back and forthto Alaska, as Ipreviouslymentioned to the Russiancoast. The Russians were not our friends at that time.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Now would you to this everyday? In other words, would you take off in the morning and go up there?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: No, no. You did other work too.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: You worked in the payroll office, you worked in different jobs.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: How many times would you do the trip up?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I only did it once.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. But did you land?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I didn't stay there.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: You land the tank?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: The tank would get off?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: The --

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: The dynamite?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: The -- no, no, the aircraft would get off. They would just leave the crews there. They were a scouring crew.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Well, I call it scouring, but it is really a crew scouring the coast of Russia to see what activities were going on. It is only 200 miles away so sometimes the aircraft would stay there, and you go up, circle around, you know.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: How long were you there?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I was there for the balance of the war. I signed up in the navy for the duration of the war plus six months.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: And then they tried to recruit you to sign up in the regular navy, and I didn't do that. I went home to Boston.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. Now you were active in the reserves, but you are also active in other activities like the American Legion.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I was very active in the American Legion. You will find pictures in there. I have pictures. I was active in the American Legion. I became the Commander of Post 1232. And then I was also president of the Management Club and Capitol Airlines at that time.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. How long have you been -- are you still a member of the Legion?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes, in Arlington Heights.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. Got your hat right here?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: The commander just made me a new hat.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. Were you commander in Arlington Heights too?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Just in Chicago?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Just in Chicago.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: How long were you the commander?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Until Midway closed.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: And then where did you go from Midway when Midway closed? You went to O'Hare?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: O'Hare, and then Arlington Heights, and I am just a member there.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. You are active?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: No? MR.COHAN:No,I am not active. I amjust friendly with them,and I work with all their items but it is very time consuming.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: To become active. You not only become active in your own post, they expect you to participate with other Legion posts.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: But the Legion was going in a bad way. As we know, veterans and people from the service were not always recognized as being the front runners of this country. And the time we spent in Vietnam and you know, places like that were not always the greatest thing in the world for some of the veterans.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: But the Legion today has gained a lot more -- even more so than the veterans of Foreign Wars I think. The Legion has brought along a lot more younger people, and they are being recognized right now as doing a lot of things in Washington for the folks, many things.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: But I remember times when the Legion was almost very difficult to get people to come in and join.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yes, I remember that time.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: And it was not good for the veterans.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: All right. Now when you got out the second time in 1954, were you still with United Airlines at the time?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I retired from United Airlines in 1986.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. In between -- I remember something about a bobsled. Tell me the story about the bobsled.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Well, we sponsored -- we were one of the major sponsors for the U.S. bobsled team in Lake Placid, New York. That's where they practiced.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: We move the bobsled and spent money with them and worked with that crew in those years until -- and I must tell you this. Politics took over that group and it became more political than it was good activity. So we moved from that and began sponsoring the U.S.A. Luge Team, and Iam forgetting,andalsobrooming.Youknow, where theyshuffle.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: I know.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: We sponsored that group, but that's like watching paint dry.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Tell us how you got involved with the Olympics.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: We were confronted by them.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: When you say "we," who?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: The people that own the logistics company that I went to work for.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Logistics all the way, right?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: That was your strong suit.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: And the owners thought that that would be a nice thing to do, good for the people, and good for them as far as being a company involved with something.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: So they were going to sponsor it?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: They did part of it. They don't take one -- just one sponsor.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: They take a whole bunch, but wewere amajor sponsor.In fact, one of the things thatwe didas a free thingto the bobsledder organizationsaroundthe world, we moved their bobsleds at our cost from country to country and place to place like Salt Lake City where they practiced out of Salt Lake City.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: You got involved because more or less your company was going to be a sponsor?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Did you get active at all? Did you go to the Olympics and watch them and participate?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. You just acted more or less as a sponsor?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: A sponsor.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: But you got your picture taken, didn't you?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Oh, with Jimmy and the rest. They all came to our events too, and I must tell you people that study them will find out they are not very well-loved. We found people in the U.S. Olympic teams sleeping in their cars. They do that as a good thing to do for the country.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Olympians don't get paid. If they get paid, they are professionals.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yeah, so what we would do, they worked out a deal where you could give some of them a job in the off seasons.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yeah, that's --

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Like a college student.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: So you were able to hire one as a salesperson. Jimmy was --

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: You have this picture here of you and who is this?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Jimmy Shay.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: What was Jimmy's Shay's position?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: He was a skeleton which meant a one-man bobsled face down, and he won the gold medal. The one that I have on.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: That was at Lake Placid.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: That was in -- that was in Salt Lake City.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Oh, Salt Lake City.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: That was taken in Chicago. Here is the name of the company too.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. So did you ever go to Salt Lake City?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: No. One of the owners went there and rode the bobsled. He said he would never do it again.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Howabout Lake Placid,did you gotoLake Placid?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Once.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Once.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yeah, the Olympics are very, very interesting.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. Now this is when you are still with United, right?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: No, I am with the logistics company.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: So you left United in 1986?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: '86, spent three years with the Canadian company, went to work for AIT Freight Systems which my son Brian is quite aware of, and two owners. And they wanted to build up the company after ten years. They were -- in fact, I am still so close to the fellows right now. They needed somebody that would be willing to travel a lot, talk to people about joining us in the franchise business. It is defranchised now. It is mostly company operated.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Good. Let me back up a bit. You went to grammar school in Boston?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I went to everything in Boston.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Where did you go to grammar school?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: In Boston.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Whereabouts?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I went to -- let me start with the name of the Junior High School.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Solomon Lewenberg in Mattapan.Alot of people don'tunderstand what Boston is madeisup. Mattapan. I wasborn in Dorchester. You understand where I am talking about?

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: You understand. It is made up --I lived inWestRoxbury for a while. We lived inMattapan.We had arestaurant in Mattapan. We had arestaurantdowntown inSouth End.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Now THESE are owned by your father?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes, we had a coffee shop on Joy Street. The Joy Coffee Shop behind the State house. My dad ran the concessions for somebody else at Suffolk Downs.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: And he just had his own. He was very active in the restaurant business.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Where did you go to high school?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I went to high school. It has changed its name since it was (? McCangars ?) which is right there in Boston, not far from the Cambridge Line, not far from Harvard College as he was talking about over the bridge. But I went there because the war was on at that time, and I felt that besides learning other subjects, learning a trade or something that would capture you would be beneficial in your future with what was going on in the world today with the ship yards and everything else being built, and that was really a very strong suit of mine being handy.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: What did your father think about you joining up?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: He didn't like a lot of things I did. We disagreed on a lot of things. That's why I left the restaurant business.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: He wanted you you to stay in the restaurant business?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yeah, from --

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Your mother --

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Run it his way only.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Do you understand what I am talking about?

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Just your mother had to sign for it, not your father?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: One signature was needed, but he was present when it was signed.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. So he didn't --

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: He discouraged you, but he didn't say you couldn't go?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: No, he didn't like it. It was very -- it was traumatic for the both of them I think to have -- they only had one son.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Did you ever miss the restaurant business?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: No, I don't think I would ever do it. It is very, very difficult, long hours, and very demanding. And I had some good experiences. I met some nice people. I was -- I am still today and sometimes my family laughs at this, but for some reason as a young boy I became a New York Yankees fan. Never lived in New York, but I really took to four Red Sox ballplayers very closely, and I have some -- Brian has bought me a great Ted Williams thing. I have a picture of Ted Williams and Babe Ruth. And I was very, very taken by Ted Williams, Johnny Pesky, Bobbie Doerr, and Dominic DiMaggio. I used to make Dominic DiMaggio sandwiches to take to Fenway Park, the little professor, and he got married to somebody in Boston. He just passed away a few years ago.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: He was in the investment business. He was a very quiet guy, unlike many other ballplayers, but there was -- I don't know if you have read that book, the Fearsome Foursome, but that was the Fearsome Foursome.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yes, I remember those. What was the third baseman, Jim Tabor.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes. I used to wait until the Yankees came in town. My dad would take me to the Red Sox games so I could see Lou Gehrig and Bill Dickey playing catch, all those people, and I was taken to the New York Yankees for some reason.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Were you a Braves fan?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I loved to go to see the Braves. Massachusetts and Boston in particular, and the Braves in particular because they were a National League team, couldn't gather crowds.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: So as a young boy growing up, they would come around to the playgrounds and give you a knot hole card. Remember the old knot hole that you saw somebody peering through a ballpark? That was similar to what they called it. So for 5 cents and a card, you could sit in the bleachers. So when the Braves were in town, we would all take our lunches and go sit in the bleachers, and watch them.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Butyou were aYankeefan?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes, sure.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: That's okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: I mean I was a Braves fan. I was a Yankees fan too. But do you remember Bama Rowell and those guys for God Sakes?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I -- I don't remember that too much.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: So now we got you through high school. Now we got you through the service, right? We got you out of the service, and now you are working for Capitol Airlines. Now we got you married. Now you had a family?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: And I had a family.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Tell us about your family.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I have four sons.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Four grandchildren, two girls and two boys. Brian has three of them, and we have four great grandchildren right now. We have three that were born here, and my one granddaughter, Brian's daughter, did a great thing. We have a little girl from -- in our midst from Freetown, Africa which is quite near -- is Brian in the room?

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: She was -- we adopted her. She adopted her. It took two years. She is with us now in the first grade, Abigail. She speaks Creole and everything else. She is doing the Veterans thing today, and she drew my picture for her first grade. She told me she started to read, and she is quite a very -- it's really something to feel and read.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: She is very good at what she does. It took Mallory one year to bring her here from Africa to do it. It is very tied into adoption agencies. (Interview interrupted for photo.)

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I would have loved to have my wife here today. My wife-- my grandson is watching her today. She has multiple myeloma. She is pretty ill. It is an uncurable cancer. We have been treating it for a long time. She has zero balance, none. She can't stand up on her own. We will be married now, next September will be 65 years.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Fantastic.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: So we went ahead one day, and I had to go to to San Diego to an international meeting in Rancho Bernardo which is part of San Diego. I took Irene with me, and we spent some extra days and looked around, and looked around, and didn't know much about it. Next year I went to another meeting. So I decided let's rent a house some winter for three months. So we tried it, and on the spur of the moment, I went out one day and bought a place. On a spur of the moment 15 years ago. I just sold it this year because my wife can't travel anymore. So we don't go there now so I am back suffering the winters here. But I stayed active in the logistics business until a month after my 86th birthday, and I -- not as a traveler, but doing a lot of things for them with people I had met around the country and the world, and it somehow captured me in doing this kind of work. And when you like something you do in this world, it is not alone -- you do it for yourself, but you want to pass that on to others. So I began to mentor people many years ago. I have a young lady in Michigan, Lori Fairchild. She lives -- she has a building she owns now. She was a flight attendant calling on the company I work for. And one day she said to me, if I start back, I know you work long hours, if I start back after my job as I work for the day, can I talk to you? She wanted to become an entrepreneur. She was about 28 or 27 and married. We hired Lori, and she opened an office in a franchise system when we were selling franchises in Michigan, and she ended up building her own building, becoming very successful, and today does a lot of government work as an unpaid thing for the TSA. She is in the early 50s now, and she is going to sell off her end of the business back to the company again, and she is trying to get placed in Washington right now. I became familiar many years ago with a fellow, Eduardo Aguirre, A-g-u-i-r-r-e. Eduardo and his sister Chicky were Cubans when Castro took over. It was an interesting part of my kind of beginning with them later on. The dad sent them both to friends in the United States at 15. She was younger, Eduardo was 15. Chicky got married in Louisiana and eventually moved to California. I am getting ahead of my story. One of Chicky's sons was working at the golf course, and I met him playing golf. Nicest fellow. And I am still friendly with him. He is married now, and he is in the logistics business in a different way, and he is married with two children now. Eduardo is his uncle. In Santa Barbara one day, I met Eduardo at a wedding. We got to be kind of friendly. Eduardo took -- worked his way up and became a very smart guy. He went to Louisiana State University, and became a top-rated banker. Now talking about doing things on your own, when you arrive in a country at 15, you know, that's something. He is married and has two children. George H.W. Bush took a liking to Eduardo and made him his personal banker. When George became President, he moved Eduardo away from the bank to Washington as an Assistant Director of Homeland Security. And when the young George Bush took over, he made -- looking at the coin, I have his coins. He made him Ambassador to Spain. He is as friendly a guy as you ever want to meet. He is not Ambassador anymore now. He is back in Houston. He has a partnership with a company called U.S.A. Partners for something. He does a lot of work in Spain and different parts of the world and he knows Washington inside out. I asked him -- Lori Fairchild, the young lady who I am mentoring and still mentoring, has a son working in Houston for TD Ameritrade. She was going down to visit him. I said Lori, you have got to meet Eduardo. I said Eduardo can cut the grease in Washington faster than I can because I don't know anybody. So they had coffee together for three hours. He is introducing her to people now, and she is trying to break the ice now to go to work there.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: That's good.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: That's how people develop, and it is all right. It's good for them.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: I want to back up a minute. I want to get a little bit more about the family. In other words, you have been married now how many years?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Last September it was 64 years.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Now you got four boys?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Four boys.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Take us through the boys, and where they are, and what they are doing these days.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: My son Michael is -- he is 64 now. He moved from here. He was divorced and moved from here to -- he is in the logistics business by the way with the same company.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Same company you were with?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: He is the most successful of anybody there. He runs the whole Perishable Division now. He moved to South Texas which is outside Dallas. He is remarried. He says he won't work as long as I did, but he travels probably ten times as much as I did. He travels continually. I mean to the point of it being a problem.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: It becomes a problem at home.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: That's what cost him the first marriage I think. He ended up living here on the lake, near the lake in Glencoe.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Who is the next one?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Brian is the next one. He is 63, and he is an attorney. He has three children, and he is married for the second time. I wasn't used to all this happening in life because it didn't happen in my life you know. Neal is in Orlando, Florida, and his wife. No children. He is in the property management business, and that took a big nosedive in Orlando and around the world because of airbnb, and all these other places, and he is there. Paul lives in Chicago and is in the logistics business but was a journalist in Washington, and found sometimes you got to walk away. He walked away from it, and he came to work for us so he works from home and does the financial end of some of the work for the Perishable Division.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Now you have four grandchildren?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Four grandchildren. Matthew is -- he is the oldest, 34. Matthew is taking care of my wife this morning until I get home, and he is the closest one of the two males to us. I will tell you why. Stephanie is the sister. She has one child, and she works in the insurance brokerage business for Chubb, C-h-u-b-b I think you spell it. Is that what it is? Her husband is an architect, and they have one little girl. They live in Arlington Heights. Matthew lives in Arlington Heights which I think is just wonderful. Their younger sister Mallory lives in New Lenox, Illinois which is almost in Indiana I think it is, and she was told me she couldn't have any children so she started on the adoption thing. And Sierra Leone, Africa. I just thought of the name, and that's where you have to fly into. Abigail comes from a family whose father was killed in an automobile crash, and the mother has older children but gave her up for adoption, put her in an orphanage. It was a very nice orphanage, and Mallory has finally adopted her. And she has taken to us and to the world just great for a little girl that's gone through what she has gone through in her young years. She is in the first grade. Somebody asked her at the house one day what class do you like the best. She said recess. She is very outspoken. She is something. So she is learning English pretty well, but that's self-satisfaction. My grandson Dustin, who is Michael's son, lives in the town next to Madison, Wisconsin, and he is in a program of 15 students -- 15 employees are in this program. They are trained to be professors. I think the State of Wisconsin has it figured out how to do these things and not be in the financial condition of some of the things we have here in Illinois. They even pay his mortgage and give him money to live on.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: What an opportunity for a young man. So they are living up there. It is not around the corner so we don't see them as often. He is married to a little girl from Poland. They have a new baby. She worked for us, and he met her. He was in our company, didn't like the logistics business. He disliked it so he got out and went back and got his Masters and was on to this program here.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: So more followed you in your business than didn't, right?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yes. Now I am going to tell you something, my wife and I sat down one day. She is an extremely frugal gal coming from some of the hard days in Boston. My wife after leaving her job and having a family, she did not go back to work until my youngest boy was 12 years old, and then she took a job teaching in the west side of Chicago in the black area, in the poor neighborhood. She has taught in two schools there. She spent the next 26 years working there, you know, and I went to work in this job with this last company which worked out very well for me. And we sat one day, and said let's see how far we can take it to having four boys go through college with no debt and one becoming an attorney with no debt, and getting married before he owned his first business. And that worked out okay. We paid off everything.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: You should be very proud.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: We took on the four grandchildren next, room and board, and everything else, and we did three of them. Nobody has a debt, nobody owes anything in books, nothing. I got to know the receivable people very well, and two went to Iowa State. Dustin -- Matthew went to the University of Arizona, and Dustin, I paid for the first year at Illinois, and then his dad did very well in our business and wanted to handle his, but I felt that was maybe cheating Dustin a little bit. We were not doing it right so we did put the money for Dustin in a trust fund for him. So we paid off eight colleges, eight college tuitions.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: That's fantastic.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I said to Irene the other day, if we do nothing else, not one of them owes a nickel to any college. I said to myself, I was not big on buying big, big houses and things like that.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: The important things.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Yeah, I found the important things to be family.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: To me the success in life is that's number one, above anything.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I watched my dad work, and work, and work, and pay little attention to what was going on in the house. That to me was backwards. You can still work hard and do a good job, but you got to make sure in my life or in anybody else's that your family feels the family. You know, I took a transfer once in the airline business to Bangor, Maine. United wanted to open up Bangor, Maine and wanted a city manager. I had a vice president call me, and said, "Herb, this will fit right in. Coming from Boston, you will love it up there." I said, "How much time do I have to make up my mind?" You have to know some of these people in the airline businesses and where they live. He said, "How about two hours. Can I give you two hours?" My wife came home from teaching school. I was off that day, and I said to Irene, "I am going to take a job in Bangor, Maine." So while I was out of the house, she sat down the four boys. She said, "I am not going to Bangor, Maine. I am not going and neither are you, and we are not breaking up. Let dad come home every couple weeks." That didn't work for me. It ended up not good. So I decided to call up my big boss, and say "Jay, I got a problem. It didn't work. I need to retire now." He said, "I will be up in a few days." He came flying up in an airplane from New Jersey. He says, "Herb, you are too young to go. I don't want you to retire. I will get you a job back in Chicago," and he moved me back. So that was -- I felt that this was going to be against everything I believed in of working alone, coming home every two weeks.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: What was good about it? You know, just picture yourself. Some people can do that, but I can't do that so I gave up that job and came back to Chicago.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Anything else you want to add before we conclude?

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: No. What time is it?

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: We have been going an hour. That's pretty good.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I think I told you everything about myself.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I will tell you I want to thank everybody associated in Lake County with this event. I think I owe you a vote of thanks. I didn't know much about this. You know how I got involved? I work out at -- I had a heart attack at 80. I had a quadruple bypass and a whole new valve system put in. I have taken my weight from 212 down to 152. I work out three days a week for the last ten years. I go three times a week and work out. I think it kind of saved me, you know, in one way. But I was inthehospitalone day, and a fellowgot talking to me,andhe keepssaying he wanted to knowa little bit aboutme.I go tothe Northwest Community Hospital in Arlington Heights to the Wellness Center. He shows up with some paperwork one day. He said, "I would like you to fill this out. I think you ought to go up and see those folks up in Waukegan." I said, "What are you talking about?" I didn't know anything about this, you know, but to me then I began to get excited about it. But I had a little mishap. Somebody took some wrong information. Not from here, from Chicago, with the autoflight.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: I am going next April.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Good. I was going to mention that to you. We have enjoyed it just as much as you have. I know your son is a little anxious to get you home with the snow.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Well, my wife is -- she gets nervous when I leave.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: We want to thank you for your service. I want to thank you very much for being here today. We really appreciate you coming. We owe a great debt to you guys. It has been a pleasure.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Thank you. You will give me some things. What do I have here? I even brought my gavel.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay. All this stuff is yours. This is the stuff you brought. I don't want to keep this. This is your letters from the --

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Students.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: This is yours. Now you will get a copy of this picture.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Will I?

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: You will get a copy of the big picture that you took with everybody.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: That's mine.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: That's for you.

sp.speaker: Dave Sullivan
sp.p: You will get a copy of your transcript.

sp.speaker: Herbert Cohan
sp.p: Thank you.
